questions.q: What is Common Crawl, in relation to datasets like C4, RefinedWeb, and FineWeb?
options: A proprietary dataset only available to one company
The foundational raw web-crawl dataset that those cleaned derivatives are built on top of
A code-only dataset unrelated to web text
A benchmark suite for evaluating trained models
questions.explain: Common Crawl is the large public raw web-crawl dataset; C4, RefinedWeb, and FineWeb are all cleaned, filtered derivatives built from it.

questions.q: What distinguishes curated multi-source datasets like The Pile and RedPajama from a single web-crawl-only dataset?
options: They contain only code and nothing else
They deliberately combine multiple categories -- web, code, books, academic papers, Wikipedia -- into one documented mixture
They are generated entirely by language models rather than sourced from real text
They contain no web-crawl-derived content at all
questions.explain: The Pile and RedPajama are explicitly multi-source, blending web text with code, books, academic papers, and reference text into one documented, labeled corpus.

questions.q: What is the difference between Common Crawl's WARC and WET file formats?
options: WARC contains raw HTTP responses including full HTML; WET contains extracted plain text (still with boilerplate)
WARC is audio data; WET is video data
They are identical formats with different file extensions
WET is the raw format and WARC is the cleaned format
questions.explain: WARC files store raw HTTP responses (full HTML and headers), while WET files provide an initial plain-text extraction that still contains significant boilerplate needing further cleaning.

questions.q: Why is main-content extraction (removing boilerplate like navigation and ads) a necessary step before training?
options: It is purely cosmetic and has no effect on model quality
Without it, the model would spend training capacity learning from site furniture (menus, ads, footers) rather than genuine prose
It is only needed for code datasets, not web text
It replaces the need for a tokenizer
questions.explain: Raw crawled pages are full of navigation menus, ads, and footers; main-content extraction isolates the genuine article/page text so the model learns from real prose rather than boilerplate.

questions.q: Why does a sourcing mistake, such as omitting an entire content category like code, remain difficult to fully fix during later filtering stages?
options: Filtering stages can add any missing category back automatically
Filtering can only remove unwanted content from what was already collected -- it cannot add a category of data that was never sourced
Sourcing mistakes are always corrected by the tokenizer
Code data cannot be filtered under any circumstances
questions.explain: Deduplication and quality/toxicity filtering operate on what was already collected; they can remove unwanted documents but cannot retroactively introduce an entire data category that was never sourced in the first place.
